Delhi High Court

Bank's mass use of one arbitrator

A borrower challenged an award passed by a sole arbitrator whom the bank had appointed alone under the loan agreement. It emerged that the same arbitrator had been given thousands of the bank's recovery cases.

Is an award by an arbitrator appointed unilaterally by the lender enforceable, and what should regulators do about the practice?

The award was unenforceable because the arbitrator had been appointed by the bank alone, following the Supreme Court's rulings on unilateral appointments. The bank was directed to explain on affidavit why thousands of cases had been sent to one arbitrator, and RBI was asked to caution banks against the practice.

Retail lenders that use the same arbitrator for bulk recovery cases risk unenforceable awards and regulatory scrutiny. Appointment through an institution or with the borrower's consent is safer.

Statutes: Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, ss. 12(5), 34, 37
Supreme Court · 2026 INSC 6

Unilaterally appointed sole arbitrators

Is an award by a sole arbitrator appointed by one party alone valid, and can the other party lose its objection by taking part in the arbitration?

The unilateral appointment of a sole arbitrator is void from the start, and the arbitrator is ineligible under section 12(5) read with the Seventh Schedule. Where the arbitration agreement itself breaches section 12(5), no appointment made under it is valid. Ineligibility can be waived only by an express agreement in writing after disputes arise. It cannot be waived by implication or conduct. An arbitrator who is ineligible lacks inherent jurisdiction, so the objection can be raised at any stage, including for the first time in a challenge to the award under section 34.

Recovery awards obtained through a sole arbitrator named by the lender alone can be set aside even if the borrower took part without objecting. Lenders should obtain a clear written waiver after the dispute arises, or have the arbitrator appointed jointly, by an institution or by the court. Lenders and brokers should review loan agreements, client agreements and pending arbitrations for unilateral appointment clauses.

Statutes: Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, ss. 12(5), 14, 18, 34 and Seventh Schedule
Supreme Court · 2025 INSC 847

SARFAESI: tenants claiming occupation

Can a person claiming an old, unregistered tenancy get back possession of a mortgaged property that a housing finance company has taken under SARFAESI?

A person claiming tenancy through an oral or unregistered agreement must prove it with independent evidence such as rent receipts, tax receipts or electricity bills for the period before the demand notice under section 13(2). Even if proved, such a tenancy does not continue beyond one year from the section 13(2) notice; after that the occupant is a tenant at sufferance. A recital in the sale deed or a letter of attornment from the borrower is not enough. The High Court's order restoring possession was set aside.

Lenders can resist tenancy claims set up to block possession of mortgaged homes, by insisting on proof of occupation before the demand notice. At loan origination, HFCs should record who occupies the property and on what terms.

Statutes: SARFAESI Act, 2002, ss. 13(2), 13(4), 17(4A); Transfer of Property Act, 1882; West Bengal Premises Tenancy Act, 1997
Supreme Court · 2025 INSC 421

Resolution of a housing finance company under the IBC

The Reserve Bank superseded the board of a large housing finance company and, as the first use of the special insolvency route for financial service providers, started its corporate insolvency. The approved resolution plan gave the benefit of any recoveries from fraudulent trading applications (section 66) to the resolution applicant, valuing them at a notional Re 1. A debenture holder objected, and the NCLAT sent that term back to the creditors. Fixed deposit holders demanded full repayment, and former promoters and directors sought to take part in the process.

Could the appellate tribunal reopen the plan's treatment of section 66 recoveries, are deposit holders entitled to full repayment, and can directors of a superseded board take part in the committee of creditors?

The plan was restored. How recoveries are dealt with is a commercial decision of the committee of creditors, and the NCLAT could not substitute its own view. Avoidance applications (preferential, undervalued and extortionate transactions) are different from fraudulent and wrongful trading applications under section 66. The plan could assign section 66 recoveries to the resolution applicant, while the NCLT still decides those applications. A vote cast by the authorised representative for a class of creditors binds every member of that class, including those who voted against. Fixed deposit holders cannot claim full repayment by relying on section 45QA of the RBI Act or section 36A of the National Housing Bank Act. Once the plan is approved, they are bound by it. Directors of a board superseded by the Reserve Bank under section 45-IE are not 'suspended directors'. They cannot attend committee meetings or demand copies of the plan.

For lenders and bidders, the ruling confirms that the special route for NBFCs and HFCs works like an ordinary insolvency once it starts, with the Reserve Bank's administrator in charge and the old board out. Depositors and debenture holders of a failed NBFC or HFC are creditors under the plan and take what the plan gives their class.

Statutes: Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016, ss. 25A, 30, 31, 43-51, 66, 227; Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934, ss. 45-IE, 45QA; National Housing Bank Act, 1987, s. 36A
Supreme Court · 2025 INSC 268

Substantial disclosure is enough

Can a life insurer reject a claim because the insured disclosed one large existing policy but not some smaller ones?

No. The insured had disclosed a Rs 40 lakh policy, much larger than the undisclosed policies and the policy in question. That was a substantial disclosure. The undisclosed policies were of inconsequential amounts, and their omission was not a material suppression. The repudiation was set aside.

Not every omission is material. Insurers should ask whether the missing fact would have changed a prudent insurer's decision before repudiating.

Statutes: Insurance Act, 1938, s. 45; Consumer Protection Act, 1986
National Company Law Appellate Tribunal

Unregistered charge in the CIRP

In a company's insolvency a creditor's security interest had not been registered with the Registrar of Companies under section 77. The question was whether it could be classified as a secured creditor in the resolution process.

Does failure to register a charge stop a creditor being treated as secured in the CIRP?

No. In the CIRP, a security interest can be proved by other evidence; non-registration under section 77 does not by itself stop the creditor being a secured creditor.

The position differs in liquidation, where registration or other proof under the Liquidation Regulations is needed (Volkswagen Finance, 2020). Registration remains the safe course.

Statutes: Companies Act, 2013, s. 77; Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016, ss. 3(30), 3(31)
Supreme Court · 2025 INSC 174

Broker-client arbitration and family accounts

Can a broker invoke exchange arbitration against a husband for his wife's trading debt, based on an oral arrangement?

Yes. Courts must read contracts practically, looking at the parties' conduct and intention. The husband's oral instructions and the joint way the two accounts were operated showed joint and several liability. Separate client registration agreements, client codes and accounts did not change this. Arbitration under the exchange bye-laws was maintainable against the husband.

Brokers who act on a client's oral instructions to move credit balances to a family member's account may be able to recover from both. This does not relax SEBI's requirements on evidence of client orders, which still apply.

Statutes: Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, ss. 7, 34, 37; BSE Bye-laws, 1957
National Company Law Appellate Tribunal

Liquidation proceeds shared by admitted claims

Secured lenders in a liquidation disagreed on how the sale proceeds should be shared: by the value of each lender's security or in proportion to admitted claims.

How are liquidation proceeds shared among secured creditors who relinquished their security?

In proportion to admitted claims, following the Supreme Court in India Resurgence ARC v. Amit Metaliks (2021), subject to the outcome of the pending Supreme Court appeal against the Technology Development Board ruling.

Until the Supreme Court decides, liquidators distribute pro rata to admitted claims among secured creditors in the same class.

Statutes: Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016, s. 53
National Company Law Appellate Tribunal

Excise and GST dues in a resolution plan

The tax department's admitted claim of about Rs 11.77 crore for excise and GST dues was given Rs 1 lakh under the approved resolution plan. It appealed, relying on Rainbow Papers to argue it was a secured creditor.

Are central excise and GST dues secured debt, entitling the department to more than the plan offered?

No. These dues are operational debts. Rainbow Papers turned on the statutory first charge under the Gujarat VAT Act and did not apply. The appeal was dismissed.

Central tax departments rank as operational creditors. After the IBC (Amendment) Act, 2026, government dues have a fixed place in section 53 regardless of any statutory charge.

Statutes: Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016, ss. 5(21), 30(2), 53; Central Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017
Supreme Court · 2024 INSC 1044

Credit card interest rates

Could the National Consumer Commission cap credit card interest at 30% a year as an unfair trade practice?

The National Commission's ruling that interest above 30% a year is usurious was set aside. It was contrary to section 21A of the Banking Regulation Act, which bars courts and tribunals from reopening a bank transaction on the ground that the interest is excessive, and it encroached on RBI's domain. Directions and guidelines issued by RBI are an extension of the statute. Interest charged as RBI's circulars allow is not an unfair trade practice in itself. The complaint was not maintainable: the trusts that filed it were not 'persons' or consumers, and no permission to sue in a representative capacity had been obtained.

Interest on credit cards and loans is set by the lender's Board-approved policy within RBI's framework, not by consumer forums. Transparency rules (KFS, APR and disclosure of charges) still apply. The bar in section 21A is written for banking companies, so NBFCs should rely on the RBI framework and fair-dealing rules rather than on section 21A itself.

Statutes: Banking Regulation Act, 1949, s. 21A; Consumer Protection Act, 1986
National Company Law Appellate Tribunal

Plan can end existing contracts

A hotel operator had a management contract with a hotel company that went into insolvency. The approved resolution plan terminated the contract, and the operator challenged the plan.

Can a resolution plan terminate the corporate debtor's existing contracts, and how far can the tribunals review the committee's decision?

Yes. The committee's commercial decision to approve a plan that ends existing contracts cannot be questioned, provided the plan complies with section 30(2). Judicial review is limited to the grounds in sections 30(2), 31 and 61(3).

Counterparties of a borrower in insolvency, including service providers and lessees, may see their contracts ended by the plan.

Statutes: Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016, ss. 30(2), 31, 61(3)
Delhi High Court · 2024:DHC:8816

Unauthorised electronic transactions: customer's liability

A bank customer clicked a link in a message that appeared to come from his bank, and Rs 2.60 lakh was debited from his account in April 2021. He reported it at once to the bank and the police. The bank said he had shared his credentials and refused a refund. The Banking Ombudsman directed payment of only a part of the amount.

Who bears the loss from a phishing or vishing fraud that the customer reports promptly?

Under the Reserve Bank's 2017 circular on customer protection in unauthorised electronic banking transactions, the burden of proving the customer's liability is on the bank. Clicking a fraudulent link is not by itself gross negligence. The bank did not show that the customer gave away his credentials, did not act promptly to block or recall the money, and its controls for authenticating the transactions fell short of the Reserve Bank's digital payment security requirements. The customer had zero liability. The bank was directed to refund Rs 2.60 lakh with interest at 9 per cent a year and pay Rs 25,000 in costs.

Banks, card issuers and prepaid instrument issuers should record the evidence of customer negligence at the time, act on a fraud report immediately (blocking, chargeback or recall) and be able to show that authentication worked. Without that, the loss stays with the institution.

Statutes: RBI circular on Customer Protection - Limiting Liability of Customers in Unauthorised Electronic Banking Transactions, 6 July 2017; RBI Master Direction on Digital Payment Security Controls, 2021
Supreme Court (Constitution Bench) · 2024 INSC 857

Unilateral appointment of arbitrators

Is a clause valid if it lets one party appoint a sole arbitrator, or makes the other side choose from a panel curated by that party?

Equal treatment of parties applies at every stage of arbitration, including the appointment of arbitrators. A clause that lets one party unilaterally appoint a sole arbitrator gives rise to justifiable doubts about the arbitrator's independence and impartiality, and hinders the other party's equal participation. For a three-member tribunal, forcing the other party to pick its arbitrator from a panel curated by one side breaches equal treatment. A party can still expressly waive the objection in writing after disputes arise (proviso to section 12(5)). The Court said the law it laid down applies prospectively to appointments made after 8 November 2024, and that this direction applies to three-member tribunals.

Loan agreements that let the lender alone name the arbitrator are unsafe. Lenders should agree on the arbitrator with the borrower, use an arbitral institution, or apply to the court under section 11. Awards by an arbitrator the lender appointed alone, without an express written waiver by the borrower after the dispute arose, are at risk of being set aside. Bhadra International (2026) confirms that such a sole arbitrator is ineligible.

Statutes: Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, ss. 12(5), 18
Gauhati High Court

Unauthorised electronic transactions: proof of negligence

After a data breach at an online retailer, a fraudster posing as its customer care persuaded a customer to install a mobile application. Rs 94,204.80 was then taken from his bank account in October 2021. He reported it within a day. The bank refused a refund, alleging that he must have shared his one-time passwords, and the Banking Ombudsman closed his complaint. A single judge directed the bank to refund the amount.

Is a customer who is tricked into installing an application negligent, so that the bank need not refund the loss?

The Division Bench upheld the direction to refund. The bank has to prove the customer's negligence with cogent material; a general allegation that he must have shared credentials is not enough. The loss arose from a third-party breach and was reported within the time allowed by the Reserve Bank's 2017 circular, so the customer's liability was zero. The bank had also not raised a chargeback.

Read with the Delhi High Court's ruling in Hare Ram Singh, the position is that prompt reporting shifts the loss to the bank unless it can prove the customer's negligence. An Ombudsman closure does not prevent the High Court from granting relief.

Statutes: RBI circular on Customer Protection - Limiting Liability of Customers in Unauthorised Electronic Banking Transactions, 6 July 2017
Supreme Court · 2024 INSC 548

Recovering from both borrower and corporate guarantor

An NBFC lent Rs 100 crore to a company, with the borrower's holding company as corporate guarantor. In the guarantor's insolvency the NBFC received Rs 38.87 crore under the resolution plan. It then filed for insolvency of the borrower for the balance. The successful resolution applicant of the guarantor argued that the debt stood satisfied and that the borrower's assets were part of the guarantor's plan.

After receiving part payment in the corporate guarantor's insolvency, can the lender proceed against the principal borrower for the balance?

Yes. Part payment under the guarantor's resolution plan does not extinguish the borrower's liability for the rest. The liability of borrower and surety is co-extensive, and the creditor can proceed against both, together or one after the other. A holding company does not own the assets of its subsidiary. The subsidiary's assets cannot be treated as part of the holding company's resolution plan. The guarantor (or whoever steps into its shoes) is subrogated to the creditor's rights only to the extent of the amount actually paid.

Lenders can file separate or simultaneous section 7 applications against the borrower and the corporate guarantor, and accepting a payout in one does not close the claim in the other, so long as total recovery does not exceed the debt. Buyers of a guarantor company under a plan get subrogation rights only for what was paid, not control over the borrower's assets.

Statutes: Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016, ss. 7, 18, 31, 36; Indian Contract Act, 1872, ss. 128, 134, 140
Supreme Court · 2024 INSC 296

Insurer's burden to prove suppression

Who must prove that the insured suppressed other policies, and with what evidence?

Where the insurer repudiates on the ground of suppression, the burden is on the insurer to prove that the fact suppressed was material and that the insured knew of it. The insurer had produced no documents to show the other policies. The repudiation could not stand.

Claims teams must keep documentary proof, such as other insurers' records, before repudiating for non-disclosure. Allegations alone will fail.

Statutes: Insurance Act, 1938, s. 45 (before the 2015 amendment); Evidence Act, 1872
Bombay High Court

Wilful defaulter process: disclosure and reasons

A former joint managing director of an infrastructure finance group received a show cause notice from a bank proposing to declare him a wilful defaulter for the group's borrowings. The notice did not enclose the material relied on, and the orders of the bank's identification and review committees gave no real reasons.

What must a lender disclose and record when it declares a person a wilful defaulter?

The lender must give the person all the material relevant to the proposed declaration, not only what it relies on. That includes material that helps the person's case. Both the identification committee and the review committee must pass reasoned orders, and those orders must be served on the person. The members of the committees who took the decision should be identifiable. The bank withdrew its orders, and the Court directed the credit information companies to remove the petitioner's name.

Lenders (banks and NBFCs to whom the wilful defaulter directions apply) should send the full record with the show cause notice, record reasons at both stages and keep the committee composition on file. Orders passed on a bare notice are likely to be set aside. A wilful defaulter tag closes access to credit and has reputational effects, so courts hold lenders to a strict standard of fairness.

Statutes: RBI Master Circular on Wilful Defaulters, 1 July 2015 (since replaced by the 2024 Directions)
Supreme Court · 2023 INSC 1076

Nominee versus legal heirs

Does a nominee of shares or securities become the owner on the holder's death, to the exclusion of the legal heirs?

No. The nominee does not get absolute title. Vesting in the nominee under section 109A of the Companies Act, 1956 (section 72 of the 2013 Act) and Bye-law 9.11.1 under the Depositories Act is for a limited purpose. Nomination does not change the law of succession. The legal heirs, or the beneficiaries under a will, remain entitled.

Depository participants, brokers and registrars can transmit securities to the nominee to complete formalities, but the nominee holds them subject to the claims of the legal heirs. Client communication should say clearly that a nomination is not a will.

Statutes: Companies Act, 2013, s. 72; Companies Act, 1956, ss. 109A, 109B; Depositories Act, 1996 and depository bye-laws
Supreme Court · 2023 INSC 1018

Insolvency of personal guarantors

Are sections 95 to 100 of the IBC, on insolvency of individuals such as personal guarantors, constitutional?

Sections 95 to 100 are valid and do not violate Articles 14 and 21. The resolution professional only facilitates and recommends. No adjudication happens until the Adjudicating Authority decides under section 100, and natural justice must be observed at that stage. No hearing is needed before the resolution professional is appointed under section 97(5). The debtor can take part when the resolution professional examines the application under section 99. The interim moratorium under section 96 stays legal proceedings in respect of any debt.

In the company's insolvency it claimed as a financial creditor; the resolution professional rejected the claim because the project documents, the concessioning authority and the lenders had treated the CCDs as equity.

The CCDs were equity. The project documents treated them as equity, they were never recategorised with the concessioning authority's approval, and repayment obligations lay with the sponsor, not the company. Instruments compulsorily convertible into shares are generally equity, not debt. The holder was not a financial creditor.

Once the sale is confirmed, the lender cannot withhold the sale certificate and make a private settlement with the borrower. High Courts should not use writ jurisdiction to undo an auction when the remedy under section 17 is available.

Yes. The plan can extinguish such security interests; the lender's consent is not required. The lender keeps its claim against the principal borrower and can ask that borrower for fresh security.

The pledgee is not a financial creditor of the pledgor (following Anuj Jain and Phoenix ARC), so it has no seat or vote on the committee of creditors. It is a secured creditor and keeps the rights of a secured creditor under sections 52 and 53 and the pledge agreement. It cannot be treated worse than a dissenting financial creditor or an operational creditor.

Where the legislature has provided a specific remedy, as SARFAESI does through the Debts Recovery Tribunal, the writ remedy should not be used. A writ of mandamus in a commercial matter against a private party needs a clear legal right, and more caution is needed when the respondent is a private lender.

The borrower must be given notice, a chance to explain the forensic audit findings and to make a representation before the account is classified as fraud. A contractor had claims against a company in insolvency that were pending in arbitration. The resolution plan did not deal with them, and the contractor appealed against the plan's approval.

What happens to an operational creditor's claims pending in arbitration when a resolution plan is approved?

On the facts the claims were preserved: the contractor was given liberty to pursue the arbitration, and its rights depended on the outcome.

Yes. If both companies are corporate debtors for the same debt, section 7 proceedings may be brought against both. A pledgor as such may not be a financial debtor, but Doshi Holdings had been found to be a co-borrower. The creditor cannot recover the same amount twice. Must a resolution plan distribute proceeds according to the value of each creditor's security?

No. The committee of creditors may distribute by voting share. A dissenting secured creditor is entitled only to what it would get in liquidation under section 53, not to the value of its security.

Lenders holding better security should negotiate within the committee; the value of their collateral is not guaranteed in a resolution plan.

Is a State with a statutory first charge for tax dues a secured creditor under the IBC, and can a plan ignore those dues?

Distributor commission is not an expense connected with winding up. Future trail commission is not an amount 'due and payable' at the time of winding up.

Is a person who takes a bank facility for his business a 'consumer' who can file a consumer complaint?

Synchronised and reversal trades

Can pre-arranged, reversed trades in the futures and options segment be manipulative, even though they are cash-settled?

Yes. Trading is meant to make profit. Where one party consistently loses in pre-planned, rapid reversal trades, the trades are not genuine and amount to an unfair trade practice. The Securities Appellate Tribunal was wrong to hold that such trades in the F&O segment cannot manipulate the market because there is no change of beneficial ownership. SEBI's appeals against the brokers were dismissed. Merely facilitating a trade is not a violation, and SEBI had shown no negligence or connivance by the brokers.

Clients who trade in pre-arranged reversals in derivatives are exposed to action even though the trades are cash-settled. A broker is liable only on proof of its own negligence or connivance, so surveillance alerts and records of client instructions matter.

Statutes: SEBI (PFUTP) Regulations, 2003, regs. 3, 4; SEBI (Stock Brokers) Regulations
Supreme Court · 2017 INSC 975

Pre-existing disputes bar operational creditors

Kirusa, which provided tele-voting services, sent Mobilox a demand notice for unpaid invoices and applied under section 9 of the IBC. Mobilox replied that Kirusa had breached a non-disclosure agreement, so the amounts were disputed.

When does a dispute raised by the debtor defeat an operational creditor's insolvency application?

If the debtor shows a plausible dispute about the debt that existed before the demand notice, the tribunal must reject the section 9 application. The dispute need not already be in a suit or arbitration. The tribunal does not decide who is right. It only separates a real dispute that needs further investigation from one that is spurious, hypothetical or patently feeble.

Suppliers, service providers and other operational creditors cannot use the IBC to recover disputed dues. Financial creditors under section 7 are not subject to this test.

Statutes: Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016, ss. 5(6), 8, 9
Supreme Court · 2017 INSC 963

Front-running

Can front-running by persons who are not intermediaries be punished under the PFUTP Regulations?

Information about trades a large investor is about to place is that investor's confidential information. A person who passes on such information in breach of duty, and a 'tippee' who knows of the breach and trades on it, can both be liable for fraud under Regulations 3 and 4(1) of the PFUTP Regulations. Non-intermediary front-running is covered.

Fund managers, dealers and anyone with advance knowledge of a fund's orders, and those they tip off, are exposed to SEBI action. AMCs need controls on order information and on staff and related-party trading.

Statutes: SEBI (Prohibition of Fraudulent and Unfair Trade Practices relating to Securities Market) Regulations, 2003, regs. 3, 4(1); SEBI Act, 1992
Supreme Court · 2017 INSC 837

Admission of a creditor's insolvency petition

ICICI Bank applied under section 7 of the IBC to start insolvency against Innoventive Industries. The company argued that its liabilities stood suspended by a Maharashtra government notification under the Maharashtra Relief Undertakings (Special Provisions) Act, 1958, so no debt was payable.

What must the tribunal examine before admitting a financial creditor's application, and can a State relief law suspending a company's debts block insolvency under the IBC?

On a section 7 application the tribunal only has to be satisfied that a default has occurred, that is, that a financial debt was due and has not been paid. The debtor may show that the debt is not due or not payable in law, but the creditor need not prove more. The Maharashtra Act is repugnant to the IBC, a later Parliamentary law on the same subject, and gives way to it under Article 254 of the Constitution. A State law suspending liabilities cannot stop an IBC process. The IBC is a complete code designed for speed; the tribunal must decide admission within the statutory timelines.

Lenders filing under section 7 need clear proof of the debt and the default (loan documents, statements, record from an information utility). Arguments about the borrower's general hardship or other relief schemes do not defeat admission. Later rulings refined the discretion to admit, but default remains the trigger for a financial creditor's petition.

Statutes: Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016, ss. 3(12), 7, 238; Constitution of India, Art. 254
Supreme Court · 2017 INSC 593

Enforcing an arbitral tribunal's interim orders

A party ignored interim orders made by an arbitral tribunal under section 17 of the Arbitration Act. The tribunal referred the default to the court under section 27(5), but the Bombay High Court held that it had no power to punish for such disobedience.

Can disobedience of an arbitral tribunal's interim order be punished as contempt?

Yes. Under section 27(5), a person who fails to comply with an arbitral tribunal's interim order is guilty of contempt of the tribunal, and the tribunal may make a representation to the court, which can punish as for contempt of court. From 23 October 2015 section 17(2) also makes the tribunal's interim orders enforceable as if they were orders of the court.

Lenders that get interim relief from an arbitral tribunal (for example, to secure a vehicle or deposit funds) can enforce it through the court.

Statutes: Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, ss. 17, 27(5)

Admission without notice set aside

The NCLT admitted ICICI Bank's section 7 application against Starlog Enterprises ex parte. The company had not been served, and the claim did not match the record.

Can a section 7 application be admitted without notice to the company?

The admission was set aside. The company must be given notice and a hearing before admission, and the claim and default must be properly shown. Costs were imposed on the bank.

Lenders must serve the application and get the figures right; defective filings delay the process and can attract costs.

Statutes: Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016, s. 7
Calcutta High Court

Hearing the company before admission

A company against which a bank had filed a section 7 application challenged the validity of section 7, arguing it did not give the company a hearing before admission.

Is section 7 valid, and must the tribunal hear the company before admitting a financial creditor's application?

Section 7 is valid. The tribunal must follow natural justice, which section 424 of the Companies Act makes it apply, so the company must be given notice and a chance to be heard before admission.

Lenders filing under section 7 must serve the application on the company. Admission without notice can be set aside (see Starlog Enterprises).

Statutes: Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016, s. 7; Companies Act, 2013, s. 424
Bombay High Court

Lone lender's winding-up petition while JLF restructures

IDFC Bank, holding about 1% of Ruchi Soya's debt, filed a winding-up petition. The other lenders, holding about 98% of the debt, were working on a revival plan through a joint lenders' forum under RBI's framework.

Should a winding-up petition by a small lender be admitted while the joint lenders' forum is pursuing revival?

The petition was dismissed. Winding up is discretionary, and the court considered the wishes of the overwhelming majority of lenders who were pursuing revival under RBI's framework.

Winding up has since been replaced by the IBC for insolvency, where any financial creditor may file on default. Ruchi Soya itself went through the IBC later.

Statutes: Companies Act, 1956, ss. 433, 434; RBI Framework for Revitalising Distressed Assets, 2014
Supreme Court · 2016 INSC 201

Proof of manipulation by brokers

What proof does SEBI need to hold a broker or sub-broker liable for manipulative trading?

Direct proof of a meeting of minds is rarely available. Civil liability under the SEBI Act and its regulations is decided on the preponderance of probabilities; prosecution needs proof beyond reasonable doubt. Liability can be inferred from circumstances such as the volume of trades, how long trading in a scrip persisted, the details of buy and sell orders and how close in time they were.

Brokers can be penalised on circumstantial evidence for trades placed for clients, especially in illiquid scrips. Know-your-client checks, surveillance alerts and records of client instructions are the broker's main defence.

Statutes: SEBI Act, 1992; SEBI (Stock Brokers and Sub-Brokers) Regulations, 1992; SEBI (PFUTP) Regulations, 2003
Supreme Court · 2015 INSC 946

Assignment of life policies

Could an insurer refuse to register assignments of life policies made for trading?

Under section 38 as it then stood, life policies were transferable and assignable. Once the procedure was followed, the insurer had to register the assignment, and its circular refusing assignments for trading was ultra vires. The Court noted that section 38 as amended by the Insurance Laws (Amendment) Act, 2015 now gives the insurer discretion whether to accept a transfer or assignment.

Today an insurer may decline to act on an assignment where it has sufficient reason to believe the assignment is not bona fide, not in the policyholder's interest or in public interest, or is for trading in policies. It must record its reasons in writing before refusing (section 38(2) and (3)).

Statutes: Insurance Act, 1938, s. 38
Supreme Court · 2015 INSC 942

RBI inspection reports under RTI

Can RBI refuse to disclose inspection reports and other information about the entities it regulates under the Right to Information Act?

RBI does not hold such information in a fiduciary relationship with the banks it regulates, and cannot refuse disclosure on the grounds of economic interest or commercial confidence in this case. Inspection reports and similar documents obtained by RBI from a regulated entity are 'information' under section 2(f) of the RTI Act. RBI's duty is to the public, not to the regulated entity.

Findings in RBI inspection reports can become public through RTI requests, subject to the exemptions in section 8 that apply on the facts. Regulated entities should expect supervisory findings to be disclosable.

Statutes: Right to Information Act, 2005, ss. 2(f), 8(1)
Bombay High Court

NBFC outside a CDR package

An NBFC had given a term loan of about Rs 50 crore to a construction company. When the company defaulted, its banks put it into corporate debt restructuring (CDR), which the NBFC had not joined. The NBFC sought interim relief, a receiver and winding up.

Can an NBFC outside a CDR package wind up the borrower or seize its assets while the banks' restructuring is under way?

The court refused to admit the winding-up petition while the CDR package was in progress. The receiver and the injunction were vacated. The NBFC was allowed to join the CDR, and otherwise had to be told before any disposal of assets.

Under the IBC a lender that has not joined a restructuring can still file on default, and RBI's framework now binds only lenders who sign the inter-creditor agreement.

Statutes: Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, s. 9; Companies Act, 1956, ss. 433, 434
Supreme Court · 2014 INSC 678

Exchange's lien over a defaulting broker

When a broker defaults, who gets paid first from the membership card and the deposited securities: the stock exchange or the Income Tax Department?

A membership card is only a personal privilege granted by the exchange under its rules. Its sale proceeds cannot be paid over to the Income Tax Department for the member's tax dues. For securities deposited with the exchange, the exchange's lien makes it a secured creditor with priority over Government dues.

Securities a broker has deposited with the exchange are first applied to the broker's obligations under the exchange's rules, ahead of tax dues. The membership card's value is not available to the tax department.

Statutes: Securities Contracts (Regulation) Act, 1956 and Rules; Income Tax Act, 1961, s. 226(3)

Wilful defaulter rules and independent directors

Two borrowers and their directors challenged RBI's Master Circular on wilful defaulters of 2 July 2012 and show-cause notices issued to them by banks. One petition was against a private sector bank.

Is RBI's wilful defaulter regime valid, and can it be applied to every director of a defaulting company?

The Master Circular is valid, including the bar on fresh credit and the five-year bar on new ventures. It has statutory backing under the Banking Regulation Act. Treating every director as a wilful defaulter regardless of role is arbitrary. Only directors shown to be responsible may be named, and promoter-directors are treated differently. A show-cause notice must give particulars of the alleged wilful default. A private bank is not amenable to the writ jurisdiction, so the petition against it was not maintainable.

Lenders must identify the specific role of each director before naming them. RBI's current wilful defaulter directions build in these safeguards: non-whole-time directors are named only where their involvement is shown.

Statutes: Banking Regulation Act, 1949, ss. 21, 35A; RBI Master Circular on Wilful Defaulters, 2 July 2012; Constitution of India, Arts. 14, 19(1)(g), 226

Exclusive charge holder outside CDR

Yes Bank held an exclusive charge over certain assets of a borrower. The borrower went into corporate debt restructuring, which Yes Bank did not join, and the CDR package proposed sharing that security with the other lenders.

Can a lender with an exclusive charge be made to share its security under a restructuring it did not join?

No. A CDR package binds only lenders who are party to it. Yes Bank was entitled to protect its exclusive charge, and the borrower was restrained from dealing with the charged assets.

Lenders that do not sign an inter-creditor agreement are not bound by the majority's decisions, but the resolution plan must give dissenting lenders at least their liquidation value.

Statutes: Indian Contract Act, 1872; Transfer of Property Act, 1882, s. 48; Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XXXIX
Supreme Court · 2011 INSC 793

Repossession by force

Can a financier take back a vehicle by force under a hire-purchase agreement?

Even for goods under hire-purchase, recovery must follow the law. The owner-financier cannot use force to take back possession on the strength of the agreement. RBI's guidelines support this. Recovery in breach of those guidelines, or of the principles laid down by the Supreme Court, will be struck down.

Vehicle and asset financiers must repossess through lawful process, with no force or intimidation. Recovery agents act for the lender, and the lender answers for them. Consumer forums can award compensation for unlawful repossession.

Statutes: Consumer Protection Act, 1986; RBI Fair Practices Code and recovery guidelines
Bombay High Court

Bondholders' trustee seeks winding up

Wockhardt failed to redeem foreign currency convertible bonds on maturity. The bond trustee filed a winding-up petition. Wockhardt argued that it was under corporate debt restructuring and that the trustee lacked standing.

Can a bond trustee petition for winding up on non-payment of matured bonds while the company is under restructuring with its other lenders?

The trustee had standing and the debt was due and unpaid, so the petition was admitted. Corporate debt restructuring with banks did not bind bondholders who were not part of it.

The same principle now applies under the IBC: a debenture trustee may file for insolvency on behalf of bondholders, and a lender-only restructuring does not bind holders who did not join.

Statutes: Companies Act, 1956, ss. 433(e), 434
Supreme Court · 2006 INSC 924

SARFAESI alongside a DRT case

Banks with recovery applications pending before the Debts Recovery Tribunal started SARFAESI action against the same borrowers without withdrawing those applications. The borrowers argued that the banks had to elect one remedy and that symbolic possession was not enough.

Must a bank withdraw its DRT application before using SARFAESI, and is symbolic possession of immovable property valid?

SARFAESI remedies are in addition to the DRT remedy. The doctrine of election does not apply, and the bank need not withdraw its DRT application first. Under Rule 8 of the Security Interest (Enforcement) Rules, possession of immovable property under section 13(4) may be symbolic; the bank may then seek physical possession through the Magistrate under section 14.

Lenders can pursue DRT recovery and SARFAESI enforcement in parallel, as long as they do not recover twice.

Statutes: SARFAESI Act, 2002, ss. 13, 14, 35, 37; Recovery of Debts Due to Banks and Financial Institutions Act, 1993, s. 19; Security Interest (Enforcement) Rules, 2002, r. 8
